summary: Gives an architectural framework for using MPLS to build packet-switched transport networks, called the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). It describes functions such as connection-oriented paths, protection and restoration, and OAM, and covers point-to-point paths. It was produced jointly by the IETF and ITU-T. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A plan for making a flexible packet network act like the old telephone-style networks, with fixed paths, backup routes and built-in health checks.

subtitle: How to build packet networks that run and are managed like traditional transport networks, using a strict subset of MPLS.

tldr.problem: Carriers want the flexibility and cost benefits of packet switching, but with the reliability, fixed connections and built-in monitoring that SONET/SDH and OTN transport networks provide.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP): a strict subset of MPLS plus a few additions, carrying client traffic over label switched paths and pseudowires, with in-band OAM, protection switching and optional static provisioning with no dynamic control plane.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational joint IETF and ITU-T framework for point-to-point transport paths only. It is updated by RFC 6215 and RFC 7274, and the detailed mechanisms live in companion documents.

facts.value: Only one label stack entry has it set to 1

facts.label: Default OAM demultiplexing
facts.value: Generic Associated Channel with a G-ACh label

facts.label: Control plane
facts.value: Optional; GMPLS signaling for paths and Targeted LDP for pseudowires

today: RFC 5921 is an Informational framework produced jointly by the IETF and the ITU-T. It is updated by RFC 6215 and RFC 7274, and the detailed mechanisms live in companion documents.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs a Transport Profile
sections.content:
Optical transport networks such as SONET/SDH and the Optical Transport Network have given carriers a high benchmark for reliability and operational simplicity. They are strictly connection-oriented, their connections may be long-lived and provisioned by hand, and they offer high availability, quality of service and extensive Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM). Carriers want the flexibility and cost benefits of packet switching without giving up that operational model.

The document sets two objectives for the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP): to let MPLS be deployed in a transport network and operated like existing transport technologies, and to let it support packet transport services with a similar degree of predictability. Some of the functions needed already exist in MPLS, while others are additions to the tool-set that should where possible also be usable in MPLS networks in general. It is a product of a joint IETF and ITU-T effort.
sections.plainLanguage: Old telephone-style networks were very dependable but stiff. Packet networks are bendy but less predictable. MPLS-TP tries to get the best of both.

sections.title: Requirements and Scope
sections.content:
The requirements come from RFC 5654 and others, and this RFC only reminds the reader of them. MPLS-TP must not modify the MPLS forwarding architecture and must be based on the existing pseudowire and label switched path constructs. Point-to-point label switched paths may be unidirectional or bidirectional, and congruent bidirectional paths must be possible. MPLS-TP paths do not merge with other paths.

Forwarding must work solely by switching the MPLS or pseudowire label, with or without a dynamic control plane, and with static provisioning there must be no dependency on dynamic routing or signaling. OAM, protection and data forwarding must operate without IP forwarding in the data plane. MPLS-TP is a strict subset of MPLS, and it excludes Equal Cost Multi-Path, LDP signaling that creates multipoint-to-point paths, and IP forwarding in the data plane.

Packet transport services must work without depending on the client or server layer, keep service levels independent of other clients' load, and hide MPLS-TP addressing and topology from clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: use the same basic road signs as MPLS, never need a map from the internet to work, and keep each customer's traffic separate from everyone else's.

sections.title: Layers, Roles and Adaptation
sections.content:
An MPLS-TP network has two logical layers. The Transport Service layer faces the Customer Edge nodes, and each client flow is tied to a single point-to-point Transport Service Instance between an ingress and an egress Provider Edge. The Transport Path layer aggregates those instances over transport paths, which are label switched paths. Only Provider Edge nodes need to know about the service layer, while both Provider Edge and Provider nodes take part in the path layer.

Client traffic reaches the network by one of two native service adaptation mechanisms: a pseudowire, which emulates services such as Ethernet, Frame Relay or PPP/HDLC, or an MPLS label switched path, which carries network-layer clients such as IP and MPLS-labeled packets. Two interface types are defined at a Provider Edge: the User-Network Interface toward a Customer Edge and the Network-Network Interface between Provider Edges in different administrative domains. The client and server relationship is not marked in the packet; it follows from the network boundary and the label context, and only one entry in the label stack may have the bottom-of-stack bit set to 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers hand parcels to a front desk at the edge. The front desk puts each parcel on a labeled truck route, and the trucks along the way only read the route label, not what is inside.

sections.title: Forwarding and Client Services
sections.content:
MPLS-TP label switched paths use the standard label switching and time-to-live processing of the MPLS architecture, unchanged. Forwarding is by the label that identifies the transport path, and a label swap is an atomic operation in which the contents after the swapped label are opaque to the forwarder; only time-to-live expiry interrupts it. Quality of service uses MPLS Differentiated Services, and both the EXP-inferred and label-inferred modes are supported.

For pseudowire clients, the stack holds a pseudowire label above the transport path label. For network-layer clients, a service label rides on a transport path. If several payload types share one service path, each needs its own encapsulation label, and if only one service exists between two Provider Edges the transport and service labels may be combined into a single entry. Pseudowires may be single-segment or, optionally, multi-segment, and because the Layer 1 and Layer 2 protocols on the attachment circuits are not carried across the network, the two sides can differ.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel gets a stack of stickers: the outer sticker says which truck route to take, and the inner one says which customer it belongs to.

sections.title: OAM, the G-ACh and Return Paths
sections.content:
MPLS-TP OAM covers continuity checks, connectivity verification, performance monitoring, and the generating, filtering and managing of defect alarms, for sections, label switched paths and pseudowires. It works without a dynamic control plane or IP in the data path, with capabilities equivalent to those in SONET/SDH, and where IP is available existing tools such as LSP Ping, BFD and VCCV may also be used.

The default way to tell OAM packets apart from user data is the Generic Associated Channel, defined in RFC 5586 and flagged by an Associated Channel Header together with a G-ACh label. OAM packets share the fate of the data packets, so if the path fails the monitoring notices at once. The G-ACh must be used only for channels that are an adjunct to the data service, not as an alternative to a pseudowire control word or to define a pseudowire type. Monitoring is built on Maintenance Entities, their end points and intermediate points, and an intermediate point can be reached by setting the time-to-live.

Some protocols need replies. A return path can be in-band, over a bidirectional path, or out-of-band, for example over IP routing or a separate Data Communication Network. The RFC recommends provisioning unidirectional paths as associated bidirectional paths when an in-band return is needed, and prefers the in-band path on co-routed paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Little inspector messages ride along the same track as the cargo, so if the track breaks the inspectors notice at once. Replies can go back on the same track or by another road.

sections.title: Control, Protection and Management
sections.content:
A dynamic control plane is optional. When one is used, MPLS-TP uses Generalized MPLS signaling for label switched paths and Targeted LDP for pseudowires, consistent with the Automatically Switched Optical Network architecture, and it must be able to run over an out-of-band signaling network. Paths and pseudowires can also be configured by hand or through a management system, independently of each other, and care must be taken to avoid loops. A control-plane failure must not imply failure of existing transport paths.

Survivability schemes include two concurrent paths, called 1+1; one active path and one standby path with guaranteed bandwidth, called 1:1; and shared protection, where one standby path is shared by several active paths. They are optimized for linear, ring or meshed topologies, use OAM to detect faults, and can switch without a dynamic control plane, with revertive and non-revertive behavior.

A Sub-Path Maintenance Element is a hierarchical path that lets an operator monitor, protect and manage part of a path, for example one carrier's portion of a path that crosses several carriers. Network management covers fault, configuration and performance functions, and where a node is managed by a management system at least one standard management protocol such as Netconf, SNMP or CORBA is required for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Paths can be set up by hand or by computers talking to each other. There are spare paths if one fails, and you can put a separate inspector on just one stretch of the road.

layers.label: Client layer
layers.detail: Native service traffic from the Customer Edge: network-layer packets or emulated services.

layers.label: Transport Service layer
layers.detail: A pseudowire or service label identifies the Transport Service Instance; only Provider Edges need it.

layers.label: Transport Path layer
layers.detail: Transport paths aggregate service instances; Provider Edge and Provider nodes both take part.

layers.label: Server layer
layers.detail: Carries the MPLS-TP frames and supplies the quality of service they need.

cells: Two concurrent traffic paths carry the same traffic.
One active path and one standby path, with guaranteed bandwidth on both.
One standby path whose resources are shared by one or more other active paths.

items.title: Default OAM channel
items.text: The Generic Associated Channel, flagged by an Associated Channel Header and a G-ACh label.

items.title: Fate sharing
items.text: OAM packets travel with the data packets, so a path failure is seen at once.

items.title: Control plane for paths
items.text: Generalized MPLS signaling when a dynamic control plane is used.

items.title: Control plane for pseudowires
items.text: Targeted LDP signaling, which may run over an out-of-band channel.
